contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Weinidog. People retrain for many reasons: after losing a job, returning to work after raising a family, or starting a new chapter following a career break. Others come to Wales with valuable qualifications and skills that go unrecognised, despite the contribution they could make to our Welsh economy. At the Inspire! adult learning awards, I met learners determined to gain new skills and contribute to their communities. For many, adult learning is more than education; it is a vital opportunity to rebuild their careers and their lives here in Wales. One of my constituents, Yassmein Hussein, completed 13 adult learning courses through Cardiff and Vale College and Cardiff Council, leading her to win the shared futures award at the awards. Yassmein's story shows what people can achieve when they have access to the right learning opportunities. But not everyone gets that chance, and many adults still face barriers to retraining. So, I want to know how the Welsh Government is ensuring that adults who want to retrain for a new career can access the learning opportunities and support they need to make that transition.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Members' Legislative Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): An NHS first Bill
contributions.text_english:
Thank you to Gwyn for bringing this debate to the Chamber. I'm pleased to contribute to this debate, which shines a light on the importance of keeping our NHS in public ownership, and not fall victim to creeping privatisation. At some point, every one of us will rely on the NHS. It has cared for our loved ones and communities in their times of need. And we must protect a service that provides care free at the point of need.

Cardiff is often a hub for specialist NHS services, serving people from all across Wales. My constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf is home to the University Hospital of Wales, Cardiff Royal Infirmary, Noah's Ark Children's Hospital for Wales and Velindre University NHS Trust. These hospitals have been caring for people from all across Wales for decades, and with roughly 700,000 people on NHS waiting lists in Wales, the answer must be to invest in our public health service.

This is particularly important when it comes to women's health. Despite making up more than half of the population, women-specific healthcare needs have historically been overlooked and underfunded. Endometriosis is just one example. Roughly one in 10 women are affected by this debilitating condition, and given concerns about the future of Wales's only NHS British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy-accredited endometriosis centre in Cardiff, protecting these specialist services must remain our priority.

Greater reliance on private healthcare risks creating a two-tier system, where those who can afford treatment get help sooner, while others who can't are left waiting for years. So, Deputy Llywydd, ultimately, we must invest in our NHS and protect its public provision at the point of need. An NHS Bill that strengthens these principles would only be a positive step forward for the people of Wales. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
contributions.text_english:
Participating in sport brings many benefits, as we all know. It provides physical health, mental health and well-being, while also providing opportunities to build community and bring people together. But barriers to participation can prevent people from accessing these benefits altogether. Sport Wales's 'State of the Nation' report for 2024-25 notes that two of the three factors most likely to encourage future participation in sport are if there were more facilities, clubs or groups in their area, and if it cost less.

There are pockets in my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, more specifically in Cardiff east, where public transport is infrequent and expensive. And with the decline in youth centres and community facilities in recent years following cuts, it feels as though this problem is only getting worse. I appreciate you've already answered part of this question, but I wanted to ask what action is being taken to measure and address transport-related barriers specifically, and how you're working with the Deputy Minister for Transport to make sure that there is participation for low-income families.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english: Effective Government is underpinned by taking a collaborative, cross-sector and holistic approach to policy development and decision making. It recognises that many of the challenges facing Wales cannot be addressed by individual departments working in isolation. Because for too long, previous Governments have operated in silos, failing to look at the bigger picture and tackle shared challenges through joined-up action. Take prevention, for example. Prevention cuts across health, housing and culture. Food policy connects social justice, public health and rural resilience. Creating high-quality jobs needs co-ordination between the economy and education. So, Prif Weinidog, I'd like to know how this Plaid Cymru Welsh Government is already working collaboratively across ministerial portfolios in a tangible and measurable way that will genuinely make a difference to the lives of the people of Wales.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: The Armed Forces Bill
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. As Chair of the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee, I am pleased to contribute to this debate on the legislative consent motion for the Armed Forces Bill. I am sure Members across the Chamber will recognise the significant contribution made by serving personnel, veterans and military families to communities throughout Wales. They make sacrifices on behalf of us all, and they should not face disadvantage when accessing the public services on which we all rely.

That principle sits at the heart of the armed forces covenant. It is a principle that the Senedd supported when considering the previous Armed Forces Bill in 2021, and it remains as important today as it was then. Members previously recognised that veterans, service personnel and their families should not be disadvantaged in accessing housing, healthcare and education, while also emphasising the importance of respecting devolved responsibilities in Wales. This Bill seeks to build on that foundation by extending existing covenant duties and bringing a wider range of public decision makers within scope. As the Welsh Government has noted, this would be the first time that both the UK and devolved Governments would be subject to these requirements. Our committee recognised from the outset that support for the armed forces community spans both reserved and devolved responsibilities. Defence itself is reserved, but many of the services that veterans and their families rely upon, including housing and aspects of social support, are devolved. That makes effective partnership working essential.

During our scrutiny, we sought further information from the Welsh Government on several important matters, and we thank the Deputy First Minister for engaging constructively with us in correspondence on the matters of interest to our members. First, we wanted confidence that the expanded duties would be implemented in a way that reflects Welsh circumstances. We welcome the assurances that the Welsh Government will continue to work closely with the Ministry of Defence and other Governments across the UK to improve co-ordination of support for veterans and service families. Secondly, we raised concerns about resources. New duties can create additional expectations and pressures for public bodies. At a time when budgets remain stretched, it is entirely reasonable to ask how any additional costs will be monitored and supported. We therefore welcome the Welsh Government's engagement with the UK Government on this issue, whilst noting that the absence of additional funding remains a matter that warrants continued attention.

We also examined proposals relating to the new defence housing service and the future use of Ministry of Defence land. Members will appreciate that housing is a matter of significant importance in every part of Wales. Opportunities to improve accommodation for service families are welcomed. Equally, any proposals involving defence land must be transparent, must respect Welsh planning processes, and must be developed in partnership with local communities. For that reason, we welcomed assurances that the new defence housing service will engage fully with local planning processes in Wales, and that compulsory acquisition powers would remain subject to established safeguards. We also welcome the commitment to work jointly with the Welsh Government to explore further opportunities relating to defence land and housing development.

The committee notes that differences remain between the Welsh and UK Governments regarding the extent of provisions that engage devolved competence. Nevertheless, we welcome the fact that the Welsh Government pressed UK Ministers for further information and assurances during the passage of the Bill and is now satisfied with those assurances. Therefore, while continuing to emphasise the need for ongoing scrutiny, particularly regarding funding implications and the future use of MOD land, the committee concluded that the Senedd should grant legislative consent. The committee therefore recommends that Members support today's legislative consent motion.

contributions.text_english: Prif Weinidog, I'd like to focus on the people behind the sports. So, Prif Weinidog, what support is the Welsh Government providing to support athletes transitioning into sustainable careers when they leave professional sport?

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Welsh Labour Debate: Further education
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to thank Lynne Neagle for bringing this important debate to the Chamber today. Before the summer recess, I raised the situation at Coleg y Cymoedd, which has a campus in my constituency, in Nantgarw. Across its four campuses, there were hundreds of prospective learners placed on waiting lists due to funding constraints at that point. Many had applied for construction, manufacturing and other vocational courses, but even now, with the term under way, 400 learners have had to enrol on their second or third-choice courses, while 40 of them remain on waiting lists.

So, we are now just a year away from the roll-out of VCSEs, the vocational certificate of secondary education, for 14 to 16-year-olds. The situation at Coleg y Cymoedd clearly demonstrates there is already strong demand among young people for vocational education. So, with just one year to go until the roll-out, I wondered how the Welsh Government is planning to ensure the VCSEs are delivered consistently across all schools in Wales and, crucially, joined up with further education, apprenticeships and the skills needs that employers want.

contributions.text_english:
I'm very proud to serve a diverse constituency in Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, with people coming from all walks of life. A more equitable Wales, where people can receive different levels of support to achieve a fairer outcome, could accelerate our ambitions for a more equal nation. First Minister, people have different starting points in life and face different barriers, so how will the Welsh Government ensure that equality and equity are at the heart of delivering its programme for government?

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Putting Women, Babies and Families at the Heart of Safety: The implementation of Call for Concern in Maternity and Neonatal Services
contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr to the Deputy Minister for her statement today. I'd like to start by sharing a constituent's experience. Megan Lewis is a recent midwifery graduate from the University of South Wales, and despite graduating with a first-class honours degree, Megan and 62 other graduates have been told that there are no band 5 vacancies for them. In her own words, Megan says, ‘We are being told we are not needed, but we are needed. I see it with my own eyes. The staff see it, the women and the families—we all see it.’

Safe staffing is not optional. I recently wrote to Cardiff and Vale health board who told me that they do not anticipate any vacancies in the near future, and are currently over-established by around 20 whole-time equivalent midwives. It feels like there's a disconnect between the experience on the ground and the staffing levels that health boards are required to maintain. The upcoming national workforce plan announced by the Government does present a valuable opportunity to shape the future of the workforce, so I wondered if the Deputy Minister could just give some clarity on how this will improve the way staffing demand and the commissioning of training courses will be aligned with each other.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. 90-second Statements
contributions.text_english:
Following Thursday's Remembering Srebrenica commemoration, attended by Members across this Senedd, we pause to honour the victims and survivors of the Srebrenica genocide. This year's theme, 'We are here', reminds us that, while the genocide sought to erase a people, survivors continue with dignity, courage and strength, and their stories continue to educate and inspire future generations.

We remember the 8,372 Muslim men and boys murdered in the town of Srebrenica alone. We remember the more than 100,000 people murdered across Bosnia and Herzegovina. We remember the 2 million people forced from their homes. And we remember the more than 50,000 women who were the victims of genocidal rape between 1992 and 1995. Because we know that behind every number is a name, a life lost and a family changed forever.

We also recognise the vital work of Remembering Srebrenica Wales. Continued investment in education, including support for more school and college visits to Bosnia and Herzegovina, is essential to ensure future generations learn these lessons and help realise the ambitions of our 'Anti-racist Wales Action Plan'. As His Majesty King Charles III said himself in his own words, by remembering the pain of the past and learning its lessons, we can together resolve that it must never happen again.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
contributions.text_english:
I'm very pleased to contribute to this very important debate, and I thank Shav and the others for bringing it forward to the Chamber.

For many young people, the question is not simply whether they can find work, it is whether they can build a future for themselves here in Wales. We rightly celebrate Wales as a great place to live, but we should also aspire to make it the best place to start your career. That means ensuring that opportunity is not determined by postcode or personal circumstance. Too often young people face very different prospects depending on where they grow up in Cardiff or in Wales. As we've heard, those living with disabilities, long-term health conditions, caring responsibilities or lower household incomes frequently face additional barriers to education, training and employment. If we are serious about equality of opportunity, we must recognise that not everyone starts from the same place and ensure that support reflects that very reality.

In my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, we see the vital role that further education plays in widening those opportunities. Coleg y Cymoedd serves thousands of learners across our region, many from communities that have historically faced higher levels of disadvantage. Its principal and chief executive, Jonathan Morgan, has recently highlighted the significant pressures facing the college currently. Despite receiving more than 6,000 applications for this September, reductions in funding mean that hundreds of prospective learners have been placed on waiting lists. Those learners are seeking qualifications in construction, manufacturing, digital technologies, health and social care, childcare and other sectors where Wales needs a strong workforce. At a time when we are encouraging young people to develop the skills our economy requires and is reliant on, we cannot afford to simultaneously create barriers to stop these opportunities. Investment in further education is an investment in economic growth, stronger communities and better life chances.

We also need a skills system that reflects both young people's aspirations and the needs of Welsh employers. Strong foundations in reading, writing and mathematics remain essential, but vocational education and apprenticeships must be valued equally and linked to clear pathways into secure, high-quality employment. As our economy changes, new opportunities will also emerge in green industries, advanced manufacturing, health and care, and digital innovation. We must ensure young people from every part of Wales can access those opportunities regardless of where they might live.

We should also look beyond our borders, giving young people greater opportunities to study, train and work across Europe, while encouraging them to bring those skills and experiences back to Wales. That can strengthen both individual careers and our economy as a whole. Ultimately, this debate is about more than employment statistics. It is about giving young people confidence that they can build fulfilling lives right here in Wales, and that requires joined-up action across education, skills, transport, housing and economic development. If we get those building blocks right, we will not simply reduce the number of young people who are NEET or improve employment figures—we will create a Wales where young people choose to stay, not because they have no alternative, but because the opportunities here are every bit as ambitious as the futures that they want to build. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Cabinet Minister, families in Cardiff already face some of the highest childcare costs in Wales, with average fees significantly above those in other areas. One constituent of mine in particular, Lizzie, recently told me that she is paying £92 a day for a local nursery. She says, in her words, 'Childcare is single-handedly the biggest financial issue for my family and the reason we cannot yet afford to have a second child. We currently pay over £1,400 a month, which is £400 more than our mortgage.'

Llywydd, given the significant childcare costs faced by many families in Cardiff specifically, it is crucial that the expanded offer reflects the pressures being felt in our higher cost communities, in addition to the needs of the rest of Wales. So, I wanted to ask: when can Lizzie and other families across Cardiff, specifically, expect to be included in the expanded offer, what factors are determining which areas are being prioritised, and how can you ensure fairness for families in higher cost areas like Cardiff in the meantime?

contributions.item_title_en: 9. Short Debate: Life expectancy inequalities in Cardiff’s southern arc
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Ahead of today's short debate, I proactively reached out to all political parties representing the city of Cardiff, and have received confirmation from Anthony Slaughter, Shav Taj and Leticia Gonzalez, who wish to contribute, and I look forward to hearing their contributions.

Members of the Senedd, a baby boy is born in Cardiff on the same night as another baby boy only a few miles away. One is born in Adamsdown, within Cardiff's southern arc, and the other is born in Lisvane. They will grow up under the same national health service, the same city council, the same education system. They will breathe the same air drifting in from the coast and walk streets under the same Welsh sky. And yet the evidence before us shows that one of those boys can expect to live more than a decade longer than the other and spend a significantly greater proportion of his life in good health. That is not fate; it is structure.

I have chosen to bring forward this contribution on life expectancy inequalities in Cardiff's southern arc because it is here that the consequences of deprivation are most concentrated and where the gap between communities within the same city becomes most stark. The picture is not simple and it is not driven by a single cause. Life expectancy trends in Cardiff over the past decade show only modest changes overall. Some measures have risen slightly and others have fallen. More recently, life expectancy has largely returned to pre-pandemic levels. And on the surface, that can appear like stability, but healthy life expectancy tells a very different and more troubling story. It has fallen over the past decade. In 2021-23, healthy life expectancy stood at 60.3 years for males and 59.6 years for females, both lower than a decade earlier. In other words, while some people are living longer, fewer of those years are being lived in good health. This matters because healthy life expectancy is a national indicator under the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, measuring not just how long we live, but how fairly and how well those years are shared.

In Cardiff's southern arc, that inequality becomes visible in its most acute form. If the southern arc were a single local authority, it would be by some margin the most income-deprived in the whole of Wales. Within it are communities in my constituency such as Trowbridge, Llanrumney, Pentwyn, Rumney and Adamsdown, where deprivation is lived through income pressure, housing insecurity and poorer health. These consequences are seen in early mortality. Between 2015 and 2024, premature death rates for under-75s in parts of Plasnewydd were six times higher than in the least deprived parts of the city. When we look at life expectancy itself, the gap within Cardiff reaches over a decade. So, to take that, the gap in male life expectancy is 10.3 years between the most and least deprived areas of the city, and for women it is a gap of 13.2 years, and these inequalities begin long before adulthood.

In Adamsdown, almost 40 per cent of children live in low-income families after housing costs, in contrast to other parts of the city where that figure is below 10 per cent. That inequality then carries forward into daily life. Around 21 per cent of people in Wales experience food insecurity, with almost 30 per cent of those in Cardiff's most deprived communities reporting that they skip meals, reduce their portion sizes or go without food completely.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution: Priorities for Government Effectiveness and Constitution
contributions.text_english:
Thank you. Cabinet Minister, the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 remains one of the most ambitious and pioneering pieces of legislation in the entire world. It gives a voice to those not yet born, ensuring that the decisions we make today here in this Chamber are shaped not only by present need, but by our responsibility to future generations. The Act provides a framework for tackling major challenges, including the climate crisis—as we're seeing this week, with the red weather warning—inequality, poverty and pressures on public services. However, its success depends on effective implementation across Government and the wider public sector.

I welcome the forthcoming 'Wellbeing of Wales' and 'Future Trends' reports, alongside the Government's commitment to a post-legislative review. These provide an important opportunity to strengthen implementation and ensure decisions are informed by the long-term challenges and opportunities facing Wales. Given these opportunities, how will the Government strengthen implementation of the Act and turn its ambition into action for the people of Wales?

contributions.text_english: Diolch. For many families, food poverty is not just about having enough to eat, it's about access to healthy and nutritious food. As the cost-of-living crisis continues, cheaper options are often highly processed, leaving most of our deprived communities disproportionately affected by obesity, type 2 diabetes and other preventable conditions. This drives pressure on our NHS, harms educational outcomes, reduces productivity, and carries out wider economic costs. Tackling food poverty is an investment in preventative health, economic growth and equality. With that in mind, will the Cabinet Minister outline the cross-Government action to make healthy food affordable, and how success in reducing these inequalities will be measured?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english: Many young people in Cardiff are facing impossible housing situations. Some are sleeping in temporary accommodation, sofa surfing, or living with constant uncertainty about where they'll stay next. We often talk about housing as a policy issue, but for these young people, it's about safety, education, mental health, and laying stable foundations for their futures. In 2024-25, more than 300 households of young people aged 16 to 24 reached out to their local authority due to homelessness or the risk of homelessness. This figure has remained consistently high over the past five years, though the true scale is likely far higher, as many young people do not identify as homeless, or do not know where to seek the support. When a young person becomes homeless, the consequences can last a lifetime. Charities and local services are working hard, but many are under immense pressure, and demand continues to grow. Can the Welsh Government outline its plans to tackle youth homelessness at its root and give young people in our capital city the confidence that they won't be forgotten?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the First Minister: The First Minister's Priorities
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. Families across Cardiff are facing rising childcare costs at a time when too many children are growing up in poverty. Parents should not be forced to choose between work and affordable childcare, and every child deserves the best possible start in life. This challenge is particularly acute right now across Cardiff, where 41.6 per cent of children are living in income deprivation, higher than the Wales average of 38.7 per cent, highlighting the scale of need in our communities. I welcome this Government's commitment to expanding childcare provision and tackling child poverty once and for all. Does the First Minister agree with me that investing in a universal childcare offer is one of the most effective ways of supporting families, boosting employment and giving children a fair start? And will he outline how those benefits will be delivered in communities across Cardiff, and, indeed, across the whole of Wales? Diolch.
